analysis.one_liner: Bans targeted advertising to kids and young teens and gives families new rights to see and delete their online data.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the bill unanimously on March 5, 2026; the House has held it at the desk without action since March 16.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updates the 1998 children's online privacy law to cover teens up to age 17, not just young children. It bans companies from using kids' personal data for individualized advertising, requires consent before collecting their data, lets parents and teens see and delete what was collected, and requires companies to secure the data. The Senate passed it unanimously in March 2026; the House received it and has held it at the desk since.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 13 and teens aged 13–16 gain: companies can no longer use their personal information for individualized advertising, must get consent before collecting it, must let them or their parents delete or correct it, and must secure it against breaches. Parents of young children gain clearer notice and control.

how_it_helps.text: Bans collecting or using a child's or teen's personal information for individual-specific advertising, including profiling and targeting based on group traits like age, sex, race, or income.
Requires clear notice and consent before personal information of a child or teen is collected, and bars collecting it beyond what the service the person asked for requires.
Gives parents (for children) and teens themselves the right to see what data was collected, delete it or their posted content, correct inaccurate information, and get a copy of it.
Requires reasonable security practices for the data and blocks keeping it longer than needed, and generally requires notice before a child's or teen's data is stored outside the United States.
Allows states to pass stronger protections, since the bill only preempts state laws that conflict with it.

analysis.who_pays: Websites, apps, and connected-device makers that serve young users, which must rebuild consent, notice, deletion, and security systems, and the advertising industry, which loses the ability to target minors with personalized ads.

drawbacks.text: The bill expressly does not require websites to verify a user's age or build age-checking systems, so a platform can avoid the rules entirely as long as it does not know or reasonably should know a user is under 17 — leaving the main protection dependent on companies policing themselves.
FTC guidance on the new knowledge standard is explicitly non-binding and cannot be the basis of an enforcement action, which limits how much the rule of construction adds in practice.

Compliance will require websites and app makers to overhaul notice, consent, and deletion systems, and small operators bear costs assessed under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, which could push some small services to restrict features for minors rather than comply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — keeping ad companies from building profiles on minors and giving families deletion and correction rights — is real and the compliance cost for most operators is modest, since many of these rules extend existing child-privacy law to teens. The honest drawbacks are that the ban does not apply to operators that do not know or cannot reasonably infer a user is under 17, so determined platforms can avoid it by not checking ages, and that FTC guidance cannot be enforced on its own. On balance the protections outweigh the compliance burden, but the bill is narrower than its billing.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it unanimously with amendments in March 2026, and the House received it but has left it sitting at the desk without a vote.

narrative.text: The Senate Commerce Committee favorably reported the bill with amendments on January 27, 2026.
The Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent on March 5, 2026, with no recorded opposition.
The House received the bill on March 16, 2026 and held it at the desk, with no committee referral or floor action since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, children and families gain nothing yet; platforms and ad networks keep targeting minors while the bill waits.

for.what_they_did: Lobbied against strict children's online privacy rules, including provisions banning targeted ads to minors, in prior Congresses; no House action on this bill has occurred since it arrived at the desk.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 21 cosponsors split across both parties (13 Democrats, 7 Republicans, 1 independent) and passed the Senate by unanimous consent, so the fight so far has split no party lines.

industries.note: The bill bans using children's and teens' personal data for individual-specific advertising, cutting off profiling-based ad revenue for users under 17. Contextual ads remain allowed, so the industry keeps a channel but loses its most lucrative one for this age group.

They lose targeted advertising and face new notice, consent, deletion, and security duties for young users, but keep contextual advertising and internal-operations uses of data. The bill deliberately does not require age verification, easing the compliance burden.

The bill lets these companies collect student data without parental consent when operating under a written school agreement limited to educational purposes, locking in their role in classrooms while adding notice and review rights for parents.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has passed the Senate and now sits at the House desk with no committee referral or floor action since March 2026. Companion children's privacy bills have historically stalled in the House Energy and Commerce Committee even after Senate passage; without a scheduled House vote before the Congress ends in January 2027, the bill is likely to die without becoming law.
